claims.text: The initial alloy is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The initial CoCrFeNiTi alloy has a simple crystal structure.
A controlled amount of carbon is added as an alloying element to CoCrFeNiTi.
Powder metallurgy is used to produce the carbon-modified alloy.
Processing includes subsequent heat treatment between 1000 and 1200 °C.
The heat treatment will ensure homogenization.
Carbon addition and powder-metallurgy processing will produce carbide precipitates.
Carbide precipitates will impede dislocation movement.
Obstruction of dislocation movement by carbide precipitates will produce precipitation hardening.
The carbon-modified alloy will have at least 15% greater hardness than the unmodified alloy.
The carbon-modified alloy will have at least 10% greater yield strength than the unmodified alloy.
The carbon-modified alloy will retain at least 5% elongation at break.
Carbon modification will preserve favorable machinability.
The predicted improvements apply over testing temperatures from 25 to 600 °C.
SEM, TEM, and XRD can be used to compare the microstructures of unmodified and carbon-modified CoCrFeNiTi.
Hardness, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation at break will be measured in both unmodified and carbon-modified alloys.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires at least a 15% hardness increase and a 10% yield-strength increase, whereas the falsification rule only rejects increases below 10% hardness and 5% yield strength. Thus, results between 10–15% hardness or 5–10% yield-strength improvement would fail the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
